newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian PM says senator probe possible later.
newsitem.headline: Australian PM says senator probe possible later.

text.p: Australian Prime Minister John Howard said on Monday that he accepted the possibility of a parliamentary inquiry into fraud allegations against a key independent senator but only if a police probe cleared him.
Opposition parties want to examine the possibility that Senator Mal Colston misled parliament in denying an expenses fraud but the government argues that Senate inquiries could ruin police work.
"Let's get the police investigation out of the way and if after that the Senate believes that there are matters that should be looked at by the Senate then let that occur," Howard told reporters.

Police are investigating allegations against Colston, an independent who defected from the Labor opposition in August last year and whose vote is crucial to the passage of government legislation. The senator denies any wrongdoing.

The proposed Senate inquiry would centre on Colston's statement to parliament that unjustified expense claims were the result of "sloppy book-keeping" on the part of former office manager Christine Smith.
Colston himself last month paid back 43 nights of overclaimed travel allowances, but blamed Smith for the errors.
But earlier this month Smith recanted her statement that she was responsible for the claims, prompting the government to ask police to include the matter in their investigations.

On Sunday the government's legal adviser, Chief General Counsel Harry Burmester, warned that a Senate inquiry could prevent material from being used in any court action stemming from the criminal investigation.

Howard said: "Surely people who want this thing dealt with properly don't want a situation to arise where somebody who might be charged with an offence ... can argue that his case has been prejudiced by a Senate investigation."
"That would be a very perverse result," he said.
Colston has been under pressure to resign as deputy president of the Senate and from the Senate itself since the emergence of the allegations. He has refused to budge.

Howard's conservative government, which does not have a Senate majority, has relied on support from Colston and another independent to pass key reforms, including budget cuts, through the upper house.
Colston was released from a Brisbane hospital last week after suffering an unspecified medical condition. He is currently convalescing in an undisclosed location.
